body.text: In brief
• A lab worker at a Russian plague research institute has died in unconfirmed circumstances.
• Russian authorities said there is no cause for alarm and the death was due to pneumonia of unknown origin.

A laboratory worker at a plague research institute in Siberia fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances, prompting authorities to quarantine dozens of people and the head of Russia's health watchdog to fly to the Irkutsk region.
The death has sparked public health fears on social media, but the authorities said on Monday the situation was under control.
The World Health Organization said that, based on available information, "the public health risk to the general population appears to be low".
New risk assessments would be conducted once further information became known, it said.

United States President Donald Trump said the death was a "big problem for Russia" and offered to help Moscow deal with it, while US secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington was closely monitoring the situation.
"Anybody that has that kind of a problem, we're always willing to help," Trump said.
What is plague?

Plague is endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak, as the bacterium that causes it, Yersinia pestis, is present among the small wild mammals in its vast wilderness and their fleas.
It is rare for Russians to fall ill with plague, however, cases occur every year in other parts of the world — notably across Africa.
Plague comes in three forms affecting different parts of the body. Pneumonic plague, an infection of the lungs, prompts the patient to cough out infectious airborne droplets.
If identified quickly, it can be treated with antibiotics. But if left untreated, it can be fatal in one to six days.
What do we know about the woman's death?
Local media named the woman as Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East.
There were conflicting reports about how and where the laboratory worker, whose age was given as 28, had fallen ill, but the authorities said she had died of pneumonia of as-yet unestablished origin.

Russia's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor told state media the institute had not found evidence of any accidents involving the handling of pathogens after rumours spread on social media that the woman had dropped a test tube containing live bacteria.
Nevertheless, Anna Popova, the head of Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Siberia for an emergency meeting over the weekend.
Professor Raina MacIntyre is a professor of global biosecurity at the University of New South Wales and an expert in infectious diseases.
She said there had been conflicting reports so far, but "the response of quarantining 200 people and locking down several hospitals suggests a serious situation".
Should we be worried?
MacIntyre, who has authored a book about the history of cover-up and denial around major unnatural outbreaks, said plague does not have the same pandemic potential as the virus that causes COVID-19.
"Natural plague is mostly bubonic, which is not transmissible between people," she said.
Instead, bubonic plague is typically contracted through the bite of infected fleas carried by rodents and other small animals.
Pneumonic plague, however, can spread between people, which MacIntyre said "may explain the quarantine of contacts".
But she said even pneumonic plague caused by an unmodified strain of Yersinia pestis — the bacterium that causes plague — would be unlikely to cause a pandemic.
"The Black Death in Europe was likely due to rodent infestations of cities and towns and mainly bubonic plague," she said.
MacIntyre said there was still too little information to know what caused the researcher's death, including whether it involved plague at all.
How is Russia responding to the incident?

According to Russian media reports, about 200 people who had been in contact with the dead woman were quarantined, parts of the hospital in the town of Shelekhov where she died were cordoned off, and an aluminium plant told its workers to wear masks.

Rospotrebnadzor, in a later statement quoted by the TASS news agency, said officials in Irkutsk Region had found two cases of COVID-19 and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with her. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.
The hospital has been placed under quarantine, mayor Maxim Modin said on Friday, no longer admitting or discharging patients, and its laboratory has halted carrying out routine tests.

Igor Kobzev, the governor of the Irkutsk region, said in a statement that she had died of "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", adding: "Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified."
He said the situation was under control and that all known contacts of the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.

Two people who were in contact with the woman tested positive for a virus that causes a common cold and two others for COVID-19, Russia's health agency said, adding that others who were tested were all negative.
Asked on Monday to comment on the case, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor rather than "rumours or speculation".
— With additional reporting from the Associated Press.
